name: Spray River Bench
notes: Climbs away from the Bow Valley along the hardpacked doubletrack of the Goat Creek Trail within Banff National Park. The grade ascends steadily above the tumbling Spray River, framed by the towering limestone ramparts of Mount Rundle and Sulphur Mountain. Riders enjoy swift rolling gravel before the trail narrows deeper into the forested mountain corridor.

name: Ha Ling Saddle Pass
notes: A demanding pitch connecting the upper Goat Creek trailhead to the High Rockies Trail, confronting riders with a fierce 21% maximum gradient over loose shale and gravel. The climb wraps around the eastern shadow of iconic Ha Ling Peak and Miner's Peak. Cresting the summit at 1,683 meters rewards riders with breathtaking views of the Canmore corridor before transitioning into Spray Valley Provincial Park.

name: Goat Pond Overlook
notes: Ascends the forested bench of the Mount Lawrence Grassi massif along the High Rockies Trail in Spray Valley Provincial Park. The summit at 1,715 m (5,627 ft) opens up panoramic vistas across Goat Pond and the turquoise Spray Lakes reservoir before descending toward the winter dog sled trails.

name: Goatview Ridge Bench
notes: Rises sharply along purpose-built singletrack on the High Rockies Trail, hugging the eastern shoulders of Goatview Peak. The route features tight bench-cut turns with maximum pitches exceeding 16% over compacted gravel and exposed granite cobbles. Riders are treated to striking perspectives of Ship's Prow Mountain towering across the shimmering waters of Spray Lakes.

name: Old Goat Glacier Shoulder
notes: Traverses the high western bench above Spray Lakes, climbing through mature subalpine fir and Engelmann spruce beneath Old Goat Glacier. The trail features sustained climbing at 5.3% with steep ramps approaching 14% across firm crushed limestone. Expansive vistas showcase The Rimwall's dramatic sheer headwall across the sapphire waters of the reservoir.

name: Blacksmith Ridge Pass
notes: A sustained 113-meter subalpine climb navigating the Sawmill trail network and High Rockies corridor along the base of Blacksmith Ridge. The trail winds through dense spruce-fir forest on firm gravel with grades stiffening to 8.6% as it approaches its 1,938-meter crest. Glancing back over the descent reveals the imposing pyramid of Mount Chester and the serrated crest of Kent Ridge.

name: Elk Pass
notes: The iconic northern gateway across the Continental Divide, carrying Tour Divide racers from Alberta into British Columbia. The initial climb winds past Lower Kananaskis Lake beneath the jagged ramparts of Mount Wintour before heading into remote subalpine wilderness. Racers transition from provincial park access roads onto rough divide backcountry track with grizzly warning notices posted throughout.

name: Marl Lake Divide Rise
notes: A sharp 6.9% climb climbing past the Marl Lake wetlands along the final paved and gravel bends of the Kananaskis Lakes corridor. Short pitches maxing at 13.7% test loaded legs right before the trailhead into raw wilderness. Mount Indefatigable's avalanche gullies tower immediately overhead, signaling the final staging area for the Elk Pass crossing.

name: Elk Pass Hydroline Summit
park_name: Elk Lakes Provincial Park / Peter Lougheed
parkName: Elk Lakes Provincial Park / Peter Lougheed
notes: The true subalpine high point of the Elk Pass crossing, climbing over 230 meters up the notoriously rocky Hydroline swath to 1,954 meters. Riders grind over loose baby-head cobbles, mud bogs, and exposed powerline bedrock with grades rearing up to 14%. The summit marks the border of Elk Lakes Provincial Park, framed by the jagged spires of Mount Tyrwhitt and Mount Pocaterra before plunging into British Columbia.

name: Elk Pass Hydroline Summit
park_name: Elk Lakes Provincial Park / Peter Lougheed
parkName: Elk Lakes Provincial Park / Peter Lougheed
notes: The true subalpine high point of the Elk Pass crossing, climbing over 230 meters up the notoriously rocky Hydroline swath to 1,954 meters. Riders grind over loose baby-head cobbles, mud bogs, and exposed powerline bedrock with grades rearing up to 14%. The summit marks the border of Elk Lakes Provincial Park, framed by the jagged spires of Mount Tyrwhitt and Mount Pocaterra before plunging into British Columbia.

name: Abby Ridge Rise
notes: A short rolling crest along the remote gravel corridor of the Elk River Forest Service Road south of Mosquito Flats. Flanked by the rugged limestone wall of Abby Ridge and Mount Tuxford, the grade climbs steadily at 5% over coarse logging gravel. Heavy logging trucks occasionally share this deep mountain wilderness valley, which serves as a prime wildlife corridor for elk and grizzly bears.

name: Mount Bingay Elk Valley Rise
notes: Descends the upper Elk Valley toward Elkford before pitching upward over a short 8.9% bluff right beside the Elk River. The gravel surface is wide but prone to potholes and washboard from active mining and forestry operations. Looking across the river valley, the sheer triangular face of Mount Bingay stands as a prominent navigational beacon.

name: Crossing Creek Pass (Bull River Divide)
notes: A grueling 717-meter mountain pass climb out of Elkford, ascending along Crossing Creek to cross the divide into the wild Bull River valley at 2,038 meters. The gravel road kicks up punishing grades exceeding 21% over loose shale, creek washouts, and switchbacks. Nestled beneath the towering glaciated massifs of Mount Peck and Mount Hadiken, this is one of the highest and most remote summits in the Canadian section.

name: Upper Bull River Bench
notes: A smooth, continuous 5.5% gradient rolling south down the upper Bull River corridor on wide industrial gravel. The road contours high along the river canyon beneath the sheer limestone cliffs of Smith Peak and Mount Hadiken. Dense spruce forests line the route, punctuated by gravel bars and rushing turquoise alpine meltwater.

name: Climb 15 (Mile 116.1)
notes: Punchy Cat 4 ascent gaining 49m over 0.5km at an average 9.3% grade (max 13.9%). Traverses unpaved on track.

name: Mount Frayn Flank
notes: A steady 5.1% gravel riser climbing above the Bull River floodplain along the western base of Mount Frayn. The wide logging roadway is generally fast-rolling but features washboard ruts that demand attentive line selection. Looking southeast, the towering mass of Mount Washburn begins to reveal its craggy avalanche chutes.

name: Mount Gydosic Ridge Cut
notes: An abrupt and punishing 10.2% wall climbing out of a river dip on the Bull River Forest Service Road. The coarse gravel surface requires seated pedaling to maintain rear-wheel traction on the steepest ramps. Riders crest a narrow shoulder under the watchful gaze of Mount Gydosic before plunging into the lower canyon flats.

name: Hartley Pass (Hartley Lake Summit)
trail_name: Hartley Lake Road / Hartley Creek FSR
trailName: Hartley Lake Road / Hartley Creek FSR
notes: One of the premier and most scenic climbs in British Columbia, grinding 422 meters over 10.9 kilometers up Hartley Pass to reach Hartley Lake at 1,535 meters. The road features rough forestry gravel, rock slabs, and steep ramps up to 12.5% that wind beneath the colossal limestone massif of Mount Hosmer and Mount Bisaro. From the pass, riders face a notoriously rowdy, brake-burning gravel descent into Fernie.

name: Morrissey Ridge Bench
park_name: Mount Fernie Provincial Park / Elk Valley
parkName: Mount Fernie Provincial Park / Elk Valley
notes: Leaves the historic mining town of Fernie via Cokato Road, climbing a gentle 5.1% paved and gravel bench above the Elk River valley. The road hugs the lower slopes of Morrissey Ridge, offering clear views of Fernie Alpine Resort and the jagged cliffs of Polar Peak. This quick roller marks the final civilized passage before riders plunge into the remote southern Flathead wilderness.

name: Mount Broadwood Pass Rise
notes: A steady 205-meter ascent following Lodgepole Creek Road through the protected wilderness of Mount Broadwood Heritage Conservation Area. The gravel roadway maintains an accessible 3.4% average grade with sections ramping up to 7.3% over deep crushed stone. Towering limestone bluffs on Mount Broadwood create an imposing natural gateway as riders enter the wild, grizzly-dense Elk-Flathead corridor.

name: Harvey Pass (Harvey Lake Summit)
notes: A major 508-meter alpine grind ascending Lodgepole Forest Service Road to crest Harvey Pass at 1,706 meters right beside alpine Harvey Lake. Gradients reach 10.1% across rocky logging tracks and chunky limestone ballast. The summit marks the high divide separating the Elk Valley drainage from the Flathead River wilderness, backed by the rugged crags of Piaysoo Peak.

name: Climb 22 (Mile 205.1)
notes: Punchy Cat 4 ascent gaining 60m over 1.9km at an average 3.1% grade (max 14.6%). Traverses unpaved on tertiary.

name: Climb 23 (Mile 207.3)
notes: Punchy Cat 4 ascent gaining 72m over 2.4km at an average 3.0% grade (max 12.2%). Traverses unpaved on tertiary.

name: Snowshoe Lake Trail Crest
trail_name: Wigwam River FSR / Snowshoe Lake Trail
trailName: Wigwam River FSR / Snowshoe Lake Trail
notes: Ascends 126 meters above the Wigwam River drainage along remote logging roads intersecting the Snowshoe Lake Trail. The track consists of chunky gravel and forestry ruts with a steady 4.2% incline peaking at 7.1%. The rugged pyramid of Soowa Mountain rises across the forested wilderness basin as riders traverse toward the Galton Range.

name: Outlier Ridge Shoulder
notes: A short, sharp 5.5% ascent along the Wigwam Forest Service Road climbing around the rugged spur of Outlier Ridge. Riders navigate loose river cobbles and graded washboard alongside the upper bends of the Wigwam River. The corridor is quiet and heavily wooded, serving as an untamed transition zone before the formidable ascent of Galton Pass.

name: Galton Pass (Phillips Pass)
park_name: Galton Range / British Columbia Crown Land
parkName: Galton Range / British Columbia Crown Land
notes: The final and monumental climb in Canada, grinding 590 vertical meters over 14.8 kilometers up Phillips Road to crest Galton Pass at 1,881 meters. The road is steep and rocky, with brutal switchbacks maxing out near 18% below the craggy summit of Poorman Mountain. Cresting the pass reveals sweeping views across the Tobacco Plains and Montana borderlands before a blistering 10-mile descent into Roosville.

name: Climb 27 (Mile 273.1)
notes: Rolling Cat 4 ascent gaining 58m over 1.9km at an average 3.0% grade (max 6.9%). Traverses Compacted Hardpack on Unclassified Gravel Road.

name: Grave Creek Bench
notes: Ascends out of the Tobacco Valley south of Eureka along Grave Creek Road, climbing through mixed lodgepole and Douglas fir on a steady 5.1% gravel grade. Flanked by Krinklehorn Peak and Deep Mountain, this bench marks the gateway climb into the remote northern reaches of the Salish and Whitefish Mountains.

name: Grave Creek Divide
landmark: Bald Mountain / Mount Lewis / Tuchuck Mountain
notes: A grueling 7.0-mile sustained grind gaining 462 meters as Grave Creek Road climbs relentlessly toward the Whitefish Range crest. Pitching up to 12.5% on coarse crushed rock, the high pass between Bald Mountain and Mount Lewis crosses into the North Fork Flathead drainage with sweeping subalpine vistas near the Canadian border.

name: Climb 30 (Mile 320.1)
notes: Rolling Cat 4 ascent gaining 64m over 1.9km at an average 3.3% grade (max 7.7%). Traverses unpaved on tertiary.

name: Red Meadow Pass
landmark: Red Meadow Lake / Link Mountain / Nasukoin Mountain
notes: Legendary Tour Divide pass cresting at 1,715 m (5,627 ft) beside pristine subalpine Red Meadow Lake beneath Link Mountain. Early-season racers frequently encounter stubborn, wheel-swallowing snowdrifts on the upper switchbacks that force arduous hike-a-bike sections. This remote pass is prime grizzly bear habitat in the Crown of the Continent; riders must carry bear spray readily accessible and maintain constant vocal call-outs through blind forested turns.

name: Crane Mountain Saddle
landmark: Crane Mountain / Beardance Ridge / Flathead Lake
notes: A massive 9.2-mile sustained mountain assault gaining 569 vertical meters as it climbs east from Bigfork and Ferndale into the rugged northern Swan Range. The route follows Yew Creek Road through thick western larch timber, contouring around the high shoulder of Crane Mountain with glimpses back toward Flathead Lake. The gravel varies from smooth graded forest service road to loose, chunky surface with steep ramps touching 9.9%.

name: Crane Mountain Saddle
landmark: Crane Mountain / Beardance Ridge / Flathead Lake
notes: A massive 9.2-mile sustained mountain assault gaining 569 vertical meters as it climbs east from Bigfork and Ferndale into the rugged northern Swan Range. The route follows Yew Creek Road through thick western larch timber, contouring around the high shoulder of Crane Mountain with glimpses back toward Flathead Lake. The gravel varies from smooth graded forest service road to loose, chunky surface with steep ramps touching 9.9%.

name: Mission Lookout Bench
landmark: Mission Lookout / Swan River Valley / Swan Lake
notes: Climbs away from the quiet waters of Swan Lake, ascending a forested bench along Mission Lookout Road toward Gildart Flats. Ramps reach 7.9% through shaded evergreen woods with views stretching across the Swan River drainage. The gravel surface is well-compacted, providing efficient rolling before riders transition deeper into the Swan Valley backcountry.

name: Whitetail Creek Spur
landmark: Woodward Point / Whitetail Creek / Swan Range
notes: A short, sharp 0.4-mile kick averaging 5.8% along Whitetail Road through the lower Swan Valley floor. The road cuts along the western slopes of Woodward Point through lush riparian forest near the Swan River. Expect chunky unpaved gravel and potholes shaded by towering western red cedar and grand fir.

name: Fatty Creek Divide
landmark: Cedar Peak / Moss Peak / Fatty Creek Canyon
notes: A demanding 4.6-mile logging road climb gaining 278 meters up the wild Fatty Creek drainage into the heart of the Swan Range foothills. Flanked by the towering avalanche chutes of Cedar Peak and Moss Peak, the doubletrack features loose stone and embedded shale with sustained 7% pitches. Water is abundant in the lower canyon before reaching the dry crest separating the Fatty and Piper creek basins.

name: Peck Lake Saddle
landmark: Peck Lake / Lion Creek Drainage / Swan Range
notes: Ascends a scenic forested saddle on Peck Lake Road out of the Piper Creek basin, topping out at 1,136 meters near the peaceful shoreline of Peck Lake. The road rolls over smooth gravel with moderate grades peaking at 6.2% through dense western larch and lodgepole pine. The tranquil lake provides an idyllic opportunity for water filtration before pressing on toward Condon.

name: Cold Creek Bench
landmark: Elk Creek Point / Hemlock Point / Mission Mountains
notes: Climbs out of Condon along Cold Creek Road, ascending the eastern bench of the Swan Valley beneath the rugged silhouette of Elk Creek Point. The 1.0-mile climb averages 4.8% on solid crushed gravel, framed by dramatic views westward toward the jagged glaciated peaks of the Mission Mountains Wilderness. Watch for active logging traffic and soft gravel margins along the narrow roadway.

name: Owl Creek Divide
landmark: Wolverine Peak / Ptarmigan Mountain / Owl Creek
notes: Steadily ascends 1.2 miles on USFS Road 9814 through thick timber along the northern apron of the Swan Range foothills. Wolverine Peak towers to the east at 2,673 meters, dominating the skyline above the dense subalpine spruce canopy. The doubletrack surface is composed of firm unpaved gravel with gentle 4.3% average grades, offering steady rhythm before the upcoming high-altitude passes.

name: Richmond Ridge Saddle
landmark: Richmond Peak / Sunday Mountain / Fisher Peak
notes: A brutal, unforgiving 7.2-mile alpine epic gaining 535 meters to crest the high subalpine saddle west of Richmond Peak at a breathless 2,028 m (6,654 ft). The doubletrack kicks brutally with sustained ramps reaching 19.1% over loose shale, baby-head cobbles, and eroded ruts that force many riders off their saddles. Riders are fully exposed to sudden mountain squalls along the barren ridgeline, rewarded only by vast, panoramic sweeps across the Swan and Mission ranges before plunging toward Seeley Lake.

name: Cottonwood Lakes Divide
landmark: Morrell Mountain / Cottonwood Lakes Basin / Blind Canyon
notes: Climbs away from the Seeley Lake basin along Cottonwood Lakes Road, gaining 165 meters beneath the massive eastern face of Morrell Mountain. The forest doubletrack features rolling gravel with punchy 7.4% kickers winding through dense lodgepole pine. The high point at 1,499 meters marks the transition from the Clearwater drainage into the Blackfoot River watershed.

name: Climb 42 (Mile 515.2)
notes: Rolling Cat 4 ascent gaining 87m over 2.6km at an average 3.4% grade (max 6.6%). Traverses Compacted Hardpack on Unclassified Gravel Road.

name: Climb 43 (Mile 535.4)
notes: Rolling Cat 4 ascent gaining 53m over 1.7km at an average 3.0% grade (max 4.7%). Traverses unpaved on minor.

name: Huckleberry Pass
landmark: Arrastra Mountain / Black Mountain / Huckleberry Pass
notes: A major 7.4-mile mountain crossing gaining 486 vertical meters up Huckleberry Pass Road (FR 418) to summit at 1,822 m (5,978 ft). The road climbs through the rugged Garnet Range between Arrastra Mountain and Black Mountain on well-maintained but washboarded county gravel. Long, steady 4.1% grades with pitches up to 8.9% demand disciplined pacing before the fast, swooping descent into Lincoln.

name: North Beaver Creek Spur
landmark: Black Mountain / Beaver Creek Drainage / Arrastra Creek
notes: A short, punchy 0.4-mile rise on North Beaver Creek Road following the high-speed descent from Huckleberry Pass. Contouring the western timbered foothills of Black Mountain, this unclassified gravel spur climbs at a steady 5.5% grade. It provides the final brief exertion before rolling onto the valley floor into the historic mining hub of Lincoln.

name: Poorman Creek Divide Ascent
trail_name: Poorman Creek Road / Marsh Creek Road (USFS Road 485)
landmark: Granite Butte / Poorman Creek Canyon / Continental Divide
trailName: Poorman Creek Road / Marsh Creek Road (USFS Road 485)
notes: A punishing 9.5-mile gravel climb out of Lincoln gaining 615 vertical meters along historic Poorman Creek Road toward the Continental Divide. The route traces abandoned 19th-century gold placer diggings before steepening into aggressive 13.0% pitches on loose crushed rock. Cresting at 2,084 m (6,837 ft) near the base of Granite Butte, it offers sweeping views over the vast Blackfoot River valley.

name: Mount Belmont Divide
landmark: Mount Belmont / Bald Butte / Marysville Mining District
notes: A relentless 8.2-mile alpine ascent gaining 523 vertical meters through the historic Marysville mining district on Snowshoe Deadwood Road. Climbing along the high shoulder of Mount Belmont and Roundtop Mountain, the route passes relics of the legendary Drumlummon gold mine. The rough unpaved surface features rocky doubletrack and sustained 9.9% gradients before topping out at 1,985 meters on the Continental Divide.

name: Mullan Pass Ridge
landmark: Mullan Pass / Greenhorn Mountain / Historic Mullan Tunnel
notes: A steep 0.4-mile kick averaging 5.8% along Blossburg Road directly tracing the Continental Divide ridgeline above historic Mullan Pass. The pass marks the famed 1883 crossing of the Northern Pacific Railroad through the Mullan Tunnel deep beneath the rocky ridge. Flanked by Greenhorn Mountain, this exposed backcountry track demands solid traction over embedded dirt and loose stones.

name: Priest Pass
landmark: Priest Pass / MacDonald Pass / Mount Helena
notes: The final Continental Divide crossing before Helena, climbing 157 meters over 2.4 miles on historic Priest Pass Road to crest at 1,827 m (5,994 ft). Utilized in the 1860s as the premier stage and freight wagon route into Last Chance Gulch, the road features broad, sweeping gravel curves with consistent 4.1% to 5.7% grades. At the summit, riders are greeted by panoramic vistas toward Mount Helena before enjoying a fast descent along Tenmile Creek into Montana's capital city.

name: Grizzly Gulch Saddle
trail_name: Grizzly Gulch Road / Oro Fino Gulch Road
trailName: Grizzly Gulch Road / Oro Fino Gulch Road
notes: Departing downtown Helena past the historic Last Chance Gulch lime kilns, this 7.5-mile ascent climbs steadily up Grizzly Gulch into the northern Elkhorn range. The narrow canyon road winds under towering limestone bluffs with an average grade of 4.1% before topping out at 1,725 m (5,659 ft). The summit offers broad vistas looking back over Prickly Pear Valley before the route descends toward Park Lake.

name: Park Lake Divide
trail_name: Travis Creek Road / Lump Gulch Road (NFR 299)
trailName: Travis Creek Road / Lump Gulch Road (NFR 299)
notes: Ascending out of the Travis Creek drainage south of Helena, riders grind up 8.5 miles of graded USFS gravel toward the subalpine jewel of Park Lake. The road climbs 564 meters through thick lodgepole pine stands, contouring the eastern shoulders of Lava Mountain at an average grade of 4.1%. Cresting the divide at 2,010 m (6,594 ft), the saddle provides immediate access to Forest Service camping and cold mountain water.

name: Lava Mountain Shoulder
notes: Climbing directly past the Park Lake headwaters on rugged USFS doubletrack, this sustained 4.1-mile pitch skirts the rocky northeast flank of Lava Mountain. Riders navigate loose granitic scree and embedded washboard with pitches ramping up to 10.9% before cresting the exposed shoulder at 2,250 m (7,382 ft). The high ridgeline opens broad vistas across the Boulder Mountains and the historic silver-mining basins to the south.

name: Lowland Creek Pass
notes: Located north of Butte within the Sheepshead Recreation Area, this short 0.4-mile climb skirts Maney Lake and the headwaters of Lowland Creek on Forest Road 442. The well-compacted gravel road rises 37 meters through open pine forest at an honest 6.2% grade. Topping out at 1,973 m (6,473 ft) beneath the granite crags of Sheepshead Mountain, the pass marks a tranquil transition zone before approaching the Continental Divide trail network.

name: Hail Columbia Gulch Divide
notes: Climbing steeply along Hail Columbia Gulch just north of Butte, this 0.3-mile gravel spur crests a 2,052 m (6,732 ft) saddle where the route intersects the Continental Divide National Scenic Trail. The rough doubletrack cuts through rocky talus and dense evergreen timber above Moulton Reservoir. Riders enjoy fleeting views of the Butte valley basin before beginning the winding descent through Browns Gulch toward the city limits.

name: Big Butte Ridge
trail_name: Big Butte Trail / Oro Fino Gulch Road
park_name: Big Butte Open Space Recreation Area
trailName: Big Butte Trail / Oro Fino Gulch Road
parkName: Big Butte Open Space Recreation Area
notes: Winding through the Big Butte Open Space on Butte northwest flank, this 1.7-mile scenic climb ascends 119 meters beneath the iconic volcanic plug of Big Butte (1,920 m / 6,300 ft). The dirt and crushed-gravel path curves along Telluride Ridge past the famous mountainside Montana Tech M monogram. At the 1,871 m (6,138 ft) summit overlook, riders are treated to a dramatic panorama of Butte historic skyline, gallows headframes, and the Continental Divide.

name: Roosevelt Ridge Pass
notes: Departing Butte southward, riders tackle a steady 4.0-mile climb along scenic Roosevelt Drive into Thompson Park, a municipal reserve nestled within Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest. The route ascends 238 meters on smooth pavement and hard-packed gravel, passing dramatic granite hoodoos beneath Limekiln Hill. Cresting at 2,004 m (6,575 ft) just north of Pipestone Pass, the road transitions riders into the remote, historic Highland Mountains corridor.

name: Roosevelt Ridge Pass
notes: Departing Butte southward, riders tackle a steady 4.0-mile climb along scenic Roosevelt Drive into Thompson Park, a municipal reserve nestled within Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest. The route ascends 238 meters on smooth pavement and hard-packed gravel, passing dramatic granite hoodoos beneath Limekiln Hill. Cresting at 2,004 m (6,575 ft) just north of Pipestone Pass, the road transitions riders into the remote, historic Highland Mountains corridor.

name: Highland Mountains Divide
landmark: Gold Hill / Highland Mine Ghost Town
notes: Following the rugged spine of the Highland Mountains on Highland Road (Forest Service Road 84), this 2.8-mile climb ascends 176 meters alongside the Continental Divide National Scenic Trail. The rough mountain gravel traverses dense lodgepole pine and alpine parks, skirting the flank of Gold Hill (2,344 m). Topping out at 2,230 m (7,316 ft) near the ghost town remains of Highland City, riders enjoy sweeping vistas across Red Mountain and the Big Hole basin.

name: Mount Humbug Saddle
notes: A brief but steep 0.3-mile gravel kicker ramping up to 12% grade as Highland Road curves around the western shoulder of Mount Humbug (2,505 m / 8,218 ft). The rocky, washboard surface requires low-gear cadence to conquer the 30-meter elevation bump at 2,164 m (7,100 ft). Once over the saddle, riders begin the rapid, twisting descent down toward Interstate 15 and the Divide valley, with the ominous bulk of Fleecer Mountain looming on the western horizon.

name: Fleecer Ridge Summit
trail_name: Divide Creek Road / Rocky Ridge Trail (USFS Road 85)
park_name: Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest / Mount Fleecer Management Area
landmark: Mount Fleecer (9,426 ft) / Fleecer Ridge Plunge
trailName: Divide Creek Road / Rocky Ridge Trail (USFS Road 85)
parkName: Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest / Mount Fleecer Management Area
notes: The undisputed crucible of Montana Tour Divide route, Fleecer Ridge demands a punishing 10-mile, 607-meter ascent along Divide Creek Road and Rocky Ridge trail to a windswept subalpine crest at 2,377 m (7,799 ft) beneath Mount Fleecer. What awaits on the western flank is the legendary Fleecer Ridge plunge—an infamous, heart-in-throat 35% to 40% descent down a boulder-strewn scree chute where riders must hang behind their saddles on glowing brake rotors or surrender to a cautious hike-a-bike descent. Steeped in Montana frontier lore, the summit gazes out over the historic Hecla mining district and the ghost towns of Dewey and Glendale before dropping toward the Big Hole River.

trail_name: Divide Creek Road / Rocky Ridge Trail (USFS Road 85)
park_name: Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest / Mount Fleecer Management Area
landmark: Mount Fleecer (9,426 ft) / Fleecer Ridge Plunge

Steeped in Montana frontier lore, the summit gazes out over the historic Hecla mining district and the ghost towns of Dewey and Glendale before dropping toward the Big Hole River.

name: Medicine Lodge Ridge
notes: Ascending the upper headwaters of Medicine Lodge Creek, this demanding 1.2-mile gravel ramp climbs 139 meters up the northern shoulder of the Continental Divide with pitches steepening to 13.1%. The exposed doubletrack cuts across barren sagebrush benches and rocky volcanic shelves under the watchful gaze of Island Butte (2,500 m). Topping out at 2,407 m (7,897 ft), this windy ridge offers vast vistas across the Tendoy Range before dipping toward the official pass crest.

name: Medicine Lodge Pass
trail_name: Medicine Lodge Road (USFS Road 103 / BLM Road 185)
park_name: Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest / Salmon-Challis National Forest
landmark: Continental Divide Border Marker / Tendoy Mountains
trailName: Medicine Lodge Road (USFS Road 103 / BLM Road 185)
parkName: Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest / Salmon-Challis National Forest
notes: Straddling the Continental Divide on the high, arid boundary between Montana and Idaho, Medicine Lodge Pass carries riders over a remote 2,348 m (7,703 ft) sagebrush saddle. The rolling 2.5-mile doubletrack on Forest Road 103 traverses windswept open rangeland with expansive southern panoramas reaching toward the Snake River Plain. After crossing the border cattle guard, bikepackers embark on a fast, dusty, washboard descent along Medicine Lodge Creek toward the critical resupply haven of Lima.

name: Red Rock Pass
park_name: Caribou-Targhee National Forest / Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest
parkName: Caribou-Targhee National Forest / Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest
notes: Crests the Continental Divide at 7,044 feet on a broad, gentle gravel grade, crossing from the vast sagebrush flats of Montana's Centennial Valley into the lodgepole pine basin of Idaho. The sweeping descent transitions toward Henrys Lake and Island Park with majestic vistas of the rugged Centennial Mountains and Mount Jefferson rising to the north. Watch for moose in the willow bogs and sudden headwinds whipping across the open divide.

name: Robinson Creek Ridge
notes: Tackles a punchy 5% pitch on mixed gravel and soft dirt across the rolling agricultural-forest fringe bordering Robinson Creek. This short rise gains the crest of a low divide separating the Warm River and Fall River drainages, offering wide agricultural panoramas toward the Grand Teton skyline on clear mornings. Riders should beware of loose volcanic gravel in corners and farm equipment along the roadway.

name: Calf Creek Divide
landmark: Calf Creek Hill / Winegar Hole Wilderness
notes: A sustained 3.5-mile gravel ascent through deep grizzly habitat on the historic Ashton-Flagg Ranch backcountry corridor, climbing 797 feet at an honest 4.3% average grade. The road winds past the volcanic margins of the Winegar Hole Wilderness with dense pine timber flanking every curve. Keep bear spray immediately accessible on your handlebars, as this wild, remote corridor sees frequent grizzly activity and zero cell service.

name: Grassy Lake Dam Crest
trail_name: Grassy Lake Road / South Boundary Trail
trailName: Grassy Lake Road / South Boundary Trail
notes: Ascends a moderate 3.9% gravel ramp directly above the shores of Grassy Lake Reservoir, crossing near the earthen dam into the Bridger-Teton National Forest. The summit elevation of 7,375 feet provides a tranquil overlook across the alpine reservoir and Mount Berry's timbered ridge before descending toward the Snake River. Prime wildlife corridor with frequent elk, black bear, and grizzly crossings.

name: Steamboat Mountain Flank
trail_name: John D. Rockefeller Jr. Memorial Parkway (US 89/191/287)
park_name: John D. Rockefeller Jr. Memorial Parkway
trailName: John D. Rockefeller Jr. Memorial Parkway (US 89/191/287)
parkName: John D. Rockefeller Jr. Memorial Parkway
notes: Paved 4.2% climb along the John D. Rockefeller Jr. Memorial Parkway ascending south out of the Snake River valley past the base of Steamboat Mountain. The smooth asphalt delivers fast, effortless momentum after hundreds of miles of dirt, framed by dramatic western views toward the northern Teton Range and Jackson Lake. Expect heavy national park tourist traffic, RVs, and narrow paved shoulders requiring high-visibility tail lights.

name: Old Togwotee Pass Trail
notes: A monumental 8.3-mile backcountry grind that climbs 1,745 vertical feet along the rugged doubletrack of the abandoned Old Togwotee Highway. Gradients spike near 9% over broken rocky substrate, mud wallows, and fallen timber as the route climbs deep into the Teton Wilderness boundary beneath Angle Mountain. The panoramic payoff at the 8,652-foot summit provides breathtaking vistas across the Buffalo Fork valley to the jagged Tetons.

name: Breccia Cliffs Approach
notes: Short, stout 5.2% paved bench on the high alpine approach to the Continental Divide along US 26/287. The towering volcanic palisades of the Breccia Cliffs dominate the northern skyline, displaying millions of years of volcanic breccia and volcanic conglomerate layers. Strong headwinds frequently funnel down the pass corridor here, demanding a tucked posture even on slight uphill ramps.

name: Togwotee Pass Crest
notes: Ascends to the high saddle of Togwotee Pass at 9,560 feet on the Continental Divide, climbing 499 feet at a steady 4.3% clip between Sublette Peak and Two Ocean Mountain. The summit overlooks the headwaters of both the Pacific and Atlantic watersheds, with sweeping views toward the Pinnacles and Absaroka Range. Weather can turn ferocious in minutes with summer snow squalls and gale-force alpine gusts.

name: Warm Springs Creek Ascent
landmark: Warm Springs Canyon / Sheridan Pass Ridge
notes: A punishing 6-mile gravel ascent from the Wind River Valley climbing 1,319 feet into the high Absaroka-Wind River ecotone along Warm Springs Creek. Punctuated by brutal pitches steepening up to 17.7%, the road works through red rock canyons, pine forests, and subalpine meadows. This demanding approach marks the beginning of the grueling, isolated push toward Union Pass where reliable water and services disappear.

name: Fish Lake Mountain Shoulder
trail_name: Fish Lake Mountain CDT Alt / Enos Creek Road (FS 544)
landmark: Fish Lake Mountain / Lake of the Woods
trailName: Fish Lake Mountain CDT Alt / Enos Creek Road (FS 544)
notes: Grinds up the high subalpine shoulder of Fish Lake Mountain, topping out at a breathless 9,751 feet amidst expansive alpine tundra and stunted krummholz. Steep rock-strewn pitches reaching 16.9% test rider traction on loose shale and embedded boulders. The summit ridge offers astonishing 360-degree views of the jagged Wind River Range and the remote volcanic pinnacles of the southern Absarokas.

name: Lake of the Woods High Point
landmark: Lake of the Woods / Union Peak
notes: A short alpine crest at 9,652 feet skimming past the pristine glacial cirque of Lake of the Woods just north of Union Pass. The open high-altitude plateau exposes riders to sudden electrical storms and biting westerly winds across rocky doubletrack. This is the final high bench before riders drop slightly into the historic Union Pass saddle.

name: Roaring Fork Mountain Divide
landmark: Roaring Fork / Upper Green River Valley
notes: Climbs 243 vertical feet at 5.7% on rugged forest doubletrack along the western descent from Union Pass, surmounting a divide above the Roaring Fork. The trail winds through dense lodgepole forest before opening to vast southern vistas over the Upper Green River Valley and the shimmering granite peaks of the Wind River Range. Washouts, embedded granite boulders, and cow ruts require cautious bike handling.

name: Flat Top Butte Bench
trail_name: Big Sandy Elkhorn Road / Lander Cutoff Road
park_name: BLM High Desert District / Bridger-Teton Border
landmark: Flat Top Mountain / Big Sandy River
trailName: Big Sandy Elkhorn Road / Lander Cutoff Road
parkName: BLM High Desert District / Bridger-Teton Border
notes: Ascends a wide 5.1% gravel grade onto a sage-covered bench beneath Flat Top Mountain south of Boulder. The road transitions from cattle pastures into arid high-desert steppe with the Wind River Range standing majestic against the northern horizon. Loose gravel and washboard can cause rear-wheel spin on loaded rigs during dry summer months.

name: Little Prospect Mountain Ascent
park_name: Bridger-Teton National Forest / BLM High Desert
landmark: Little Prospect Mountain / Wind River Foothills
parkName: Bridger-Teton National Forest / BLM High Desert
notes: Steady 1.6-mile, 361-foot climb up the historic Lander Cutoff of the Oregon Trail, rising along the western flank of Little Prospect Mountain to 8,048 feet. Emigrant wagon ruts and historical trail markers dot the sagebrush meadows alongside the doubletrack. The summit crest affords expansive views across the Big Sandy river basin toward the southern Wind River wilderness peaks.

name: Block and Tackle Hill Crest
trail_name: Lander Cutoff Road / Big Sandy Opening Road
landmark: Block and Tackle Hill / Sweetwater Overlook
trailName: Lander Cutoff Road / Big Sandy Opening Road
notes: A steep 5.9% pitch climbing over an 8,133-foot ridge along the historic Lander Cutoff near Block and Tackle Hill, so named by 19th-century emigrants who had to winch wagons up the rocky slopes. The rough dirt and gravel road winds through scattered aspen groves and sagebrush, giving way to sweeping views toward the Sweetwater River basin. Ruts and loose cobbles demand careful line choice.

name: Hermit Gulch Ridge
trail_name: South Pass City Road / Atlantic City Road
park_name: South Pass City State Historic Site / BLM Lander Field Office
trailName: South Pass City Road / Atlantic City Road
parkName: South Pass City State Historic Site / BLM Lander Field Office
notes: A winding 4.3% gravel grind ascending 335 vertical feet out of the Willow Creek canyon above historic South Pass City, a preserved 1860s gold-rush boomtown. Gradients briefly spike to 9.7% over rough doubletrack and loose quartzite stones that will challenge tired legs. The ridge crest offers scenic vistas over old mine shafts, historic flumes, and the gold-rich gulches of the Sweetwater mining district.

name: Carissa Mine Ridge
notes: Stout 7.2% dirt push cresting a high 8,173-foot shoulder between South Pass City and Atlantic City, passing directly adjacent to the historic Carissa Gold Mine. The red dirt road becomes treacherous and impassable gumbo when wet, clumping onto tires and jamming derailleurs within yards. In dry conditions, it provides a brisk, panoramic climb over the heart of Wyoming's historic mining country.

name: Atlantic Gulch Divide
notes: Climbs 312 feet at 4.3% away from the rustic mining outpost of Atlantic City, following the Continental Divide Trail corridor over the ridge dividing Atlantic Gulch and Rock Creek. Steep pitches exceeding 10% test riders right out of town before leveling out onto a high sage bench beneath Roundtop Mountain. Top off water bladders completely in Atlantic City, as this is the final reliable civilized water source before entering the waterless Great Divide Basin.

name: Oregon Buttes Gateway
park_name: Great Divide Basin BLM / Red Desert
parkName: Great Divide Basin BLM / Red Desert
notes: Ascends a 5.1% gravel rise along the Riverview Cutoff to an elevation of 7,379 feet, opening the vast, arid gateway into the Great Divide Basin. The iconic flat-topped landmark of the Oregon Buttes stands prominently on the western horizon, serving as a navigation beacon for indigenous tribes and historic wagon trains. Loose gravel and frequent southwesterly crosswinds demand strong focus and paced cadence.

name: Cyclone Rim Divide
park_name: Great Divide Basin (BLM Rawlins Field Office)
parkName: Great Divide Basin (BLM Rawlins Field Office)
notes: A rolling 4.6% climb across the remote interior of the Great Divide Basin, cresting the subtle divide of Cyclone Rim at 7,372 feet above dry alkali flats and McKay Reservoirs. In this vast endorheic basin, water drains internally to desert playas rather than to either ocean, creating an eerie, wind-scoured isolation. Relentless desert winds, total sun exposure, and lack of potable water make this one of the Tour Divide's most psychologically demanding stretches.

name: Five Buttes Pass
park_name: Red Desert / BLM Rawlins Field Office
parkName: Red Desert / BLM Rawlins Field Office
notes: A gradual 2.5-mile, 476-foot climb traversing the high sage desert between the striking volcanic and sandstone towers of Five Buttes and Lone Butte. The 3.5% average gradient is deceptive as relentless washboard and sudden steep pitches near 7.5% sapped by desert heat demand steady pacing. Cresting at 7,142 feet, riders enjoy wide vistas south toward the rising forested silhouette of the Sierra Madre.

name: Smith Rim Bench
notes: Short 5% gravel climb hugging the bench of Smith Rim south of Savery near the Wyoming-Colorado border. The road winds between lush hay meadows and rugged sandstone bluffs along the Slater Creek drainage with Long Mountain rising to the south. Fine agricultural gravel provides fast rolling, though dust from livestock trucks can be blinding on hot afternoons.

name: Camel Back Ridge
landmark: Camel Back Mountain / Bible Back Mountain
notes: A steep 9.6% dirt and gravel wall pitching upward between the twin rocky summits of Camel Back Mountain and Bible Back Mountain. Riders must grind out 157 vertical feet on loose, rocky track in just three-tenths of a mile, requiring high torque and forward weight distribution. The summit crest offers stunning views across the verdant Slater Creek valley to the Wyoming-Colorado state line.

name: Brush Mountain Pass
park_name: Medicine Bow-Routt National Forest / Sierra Madre Range
parkName: Medicine Bow-Routt National Forest / Sierra Madre Range
notes: A sustained 1.9-mile gravel climb gaining 394 feet up the shoulder of Brush Mountain to top out at 8,061 feet, marking the final mountain climb in Wyoming. Gradients pitch up to 9.6% through dense aspen forests and mountain meadows flanked by Sawtooth Mountain. Just over the crest lies the famous Brush Mountain Lodge, legendary among Tour Divide racers for its hospitality, hot food, and welcoming respite before crossing into Colorado.

name: Pilot Knob Divide
notes: Climbs along Routt County Road 80 across the high sagebrush-and-aspen bench beneath Pilot Knob and Quaker Mountain. The steady 4.1% gravel grade traverses open cattle country and national forest borders before topping out at 8,612 feet with sweeping vistas over northern Routt County. The descent leads swiftly toward the Elk River Valley and the ranching settlement of Clark.

name: Bull Hill Saddle
notes: Tackles a sharp gravel rise on Routt County Road 56 as the route curves around the western flank of Bull Hill. Gradients kick briefly up to 8.5% on loose, sun-baked washboard between private cattle pastures. Reaching the crest at 7,454 feet reveals distant views of the Elk River basin and the jagged timberline ridges of the Mount Zirkel Wilderness.

name: Wolf Mountain Ridge
notes: A demanding 3.3-mile gravel ascent on Routt County Road 56 scaling the northern shoulder of Wolf Mountain. Gradients ramp aggressively through dense aspen groves and cattle guards, peaking at a steep 13.5% pitch near the upper switchbacks. The 8,232-foot summit delivers spectacular panoramas across the Elk River Valley before dropping steeply into Clark.

name: Sleeping Giant Bench
park_name: Routt National Forest / Elk River Valley
parkName: Routt National Forest / Elk River Valley
notes: A punchy gravel roller along Routt County Road 46 rolling past the historic hamlet of Mystic. The short 5.7% climb skirts the lower foothills directly beneath the iconic profile of Elk Mountain, locally renowned as The Sleeping Giant. Riders crest at 6,886 feet amidst open hayfields before rolling toward the Yampa Valley and Steamboat Springs.

name: Lake Catamount Overlook
park_name: Yampa River Valley / Routt National Forest
parkName: Yampa River Valley / Routt National Forest
notes: Ascends a short, scenic bluff on Routt County Road 14B just above Lake Catamount along the Upper Yampa River basin. The smooth hardpack surface rises at an average 5.3% grade through open meadows and ranch fences. Summiting at 7,067 feet provides an expansive vantage over the lake's blue waters and the Flat Tops in the southern distance.

name: Stagecoach Reservoir Ridge
park_name: Stagecoach State Park / Routt National Forest
parkName: Stagecoach State Park / Routt National Forest
notes: Rises steadily along Routt County Road 18 on the bluff overlooking Stagecoach Reservoir and State Park. The compacted gravel surface climbs at 5.2% past sagebrush slopes and lakeside access trails. At 7,238 feet, the crest opens up views of the reservoir's inlets and the volcanic plugs dotting the Yampa River headwaters.

name: Simpson Mountain Pass
notes: A moderate 1.9-mile grind on Routt County Road 16 climbing into the pine and aspen forests along the western base of Simpson Mountain. Gradients hover around 4.3% with occasional washboard corners that demand steady cadence. Cresting at 7,953 feet, the route bridges the Morrison Creek drainage before rolling southwest toward the town of Yampa.

name: Lynx Pass
notes: Ascends Routt County Road 16 and Forest Road 270 on a sustained 3.3-mile gravel climb to the crest of Lynx Pass at 9,029 feet. The tree-canopied road winds through dense lodgepole pine and quaking aspen with pitches reaching 9.4%. The summit hosts a remote USFS campground and marks the watershed divide between the Yampa and Colorado River basins.

name: Blacktail Creek Ridge
park_name: Routt National Forest / Gore Pass Area
parkName: Routt National Forest / Gore Pass Area
notes: Traverses high forest service doubletrack on Forest Road 212.1 just south of the Highway 134 corridor near Gore Pass. The 1.3-mile grade ascends through cool evergreen stands along the upper Blacktail Creek basin, topping out at 9,088 feet. Riders are treated to distant glimpses of the rugged Gore Range crags before embarking on the long, rugged descent toward Radium.

name: Big Park Creek Divide
park_name: Routt National Forest / BLM Kremmling Field Office
parkName: Routt National Forest / BLM Kremmling Field Office
notes: A sharp 0.4-mile gravel rise on County Road 11 climbing out of the Big Park Creek depression on the approach to Radium. The rough, rocky doubletrack pitches up to 8.4% through scrub oak and sagebrush clearings. Reaching the crest at 8,832 feet affords clear sightlines down the expanding canyon country leading toward the Colorado River.

name: French Creek Gulch
notes: Climbs steeply out of the French Creek drainage on rocky Routt National Forest doubletrack along Blacktail Road. The 6.8% average grade features loose stones and exposed ruts that test traction on tired legs. Cresting at 8,671 feet, the bench rewards riders with sweeping southern views into the remote canyons of the upper Colorado River basin.

name: Little Blacktail Bench
notes: Follows a continuous stair-step undulating bench along Blacktail Road overlooking Little Blacktail Creek. The steady 5.3% grade runs through stands of pinyon, juniper, and scattered Douglas fir on hardpacked dirt. The 8,648-foot crest marks the transition into the arid, canyon-carved terrain bordering Grand County.

name: Azure Mountain Ridge
park_name: BLM Colorado River Valley Field Office
parkName: BLM Colorado River Valley Field Office
notes: Scales the final high desert bench along Blacktail Road before the dramatic descent into the Colorado River corridor. A stout 7.6% gradient pushes riders up through sandstone outcrops and pinyon-juniper woodland to 8,556 feet. From the crest, the canyon floor drops sharply away, revealing the serpentine Colorado River and the cliffs around Radium Hot Springs.

name: Radium Colorado River Bluff
park_name: Upper Colorado River Special Recreation Management Area (BLM)
parkName: Upper Colorado River Special Recreation Management Area (BLM)
notes: Climbs away from the Colorado River bridge and Radium Hot Springs along Grand County Road 111. The 5.8% gravel slope winds up desert canyon terraces of red shale and volcanic basalt. Reaching 7,205 feet provides an iconic rearward view of the Colorado River canyon, rafters navigating Muggs Blowout rapid, and the historic Radium railroad siding.

name: Sheephorn Creek Bench
notes: Begins the notorious Trough Road (Grand County Road 1) grind, ascending 3.4 miles alongside Sheephorn Creek under the towering shadow of Sheephorn Mountain. The hardpacked clay-and-gravel surface can turn slick as ice in rain or bake into punishing washboard under summer sun. Topping out at 7,657 feet, the road winds through high sagebrush plateau country toward Gore Canyon.

name: Gore Canyon Overlook
park_name: Upper Colorado River SRMA / BLM Kremmling Field Office
parkName: Upper Colorado River SRMA / BLM Kremmling Field Office
notes: The crowning 5.4-mile ascent of Trough Road (Grand County Road 1) cresting at 8,323 feet high above the sheer 1,000-foot granite chasm of Gore Canyon. The wide gravel route traverses wind-blasted sagebrush ridges where hot crosswinds and heavy dust frequently batter riders. The summit offers breathtaking panoramas of the Gore Range before a high-speed descent drops into the ranching hub of Kremmling.

name: Ute Pass
trail_name: Ute Pass Road (Grand CR 3 / Summit CR 15)
trailName: Ute Pass Road (Grand CR 3 / Summit CR 15)
notes: A scenic 5.5-mile paved climb ascending Ute Pass Road over the crest of the Williams Fork Mountains at 9,583 feet. The gentle 3.6% grade winds past dense lodgepole pine and aspen groves with the towering 12,274-foot pyramid of Ute Peak standing sentinel to the south. Crossing from Grand into Summit County at the pass unlocks a sensational sweeping panorama of the snowcapped Gore Range and the Blue River Valley.

name: Ute Pass
trail_name: Ute Pass Road (Grand CR 3 / Summit CR 15)
trailName: Ute Pass Road (Grand CR 3 / Summit CR 15)
notes: A scenic 5.5-mile paved climb ascending Ute Pass Road over the crest of the Williams Fork Mountains at 9,583 feet. The gentle 3.6% grade winds past dense lodgepole pine and aspen groves with the towering 12,274-foot pyramid of Ute Peak standing sentinel to the south. Crossing from Grand into Summit County at the pass unlocks a sensational sweeping panorama of the snowcapped Gore Range and the Blue River Valley.

name: Boreas Pass
trail_name: Boreas Pass Road (Summit CR 10 / Park CR 33)
trailName: Boreas Pass Road (Summit CR 10 / Park CR 33)
notes: Following the legendary 1882 narrow-gauge grade of the Denver, South Park and Pacific Railroad, this iconic 15.2-mile climb ascends steadily at an engineered 2.9% railroad gradient from Breckenridge to the Continental Divide at 11,481 feet. Passing the restored Baker's Tank and timberline snowshed remnants, the road breaks into open alpine tundra beneath Boreas Mountain and Mount Guyot with immense vistas across the Tenmile Range and the vast expanse of South Park. The exposed summit at the historic Section House is notorious for ferocious afternoon lightning storms, biting winds, and sudden snow squalls that require swift tactical transit.

name: Climb 107 (Mile 1709.0)
notes: Steady Cat 3 ascent gaining 71m over 1.8km at an average 3.8% grade (max 4.8%). Traverses Compacted Hardpack on Unclassified Gravel Road.

name: Pike-San Isabel Mesa
park_name: South Park Basin / Pike National Forest
landmark: Thirtynine Mile Mountain & South Park Basin
parkName: South Park Basin / Pike National Forest
notes: Ascends a windswept plateau rise through Pike-San Isabel Village on the approach to the remote outpost of Hartsel in the heart of South Park. The 0.6-mile 5.3% pitch rolls across open, treeless grassland exposed to punishing headwinds at an elevation of 9,282 feet. Cresting the mesa opens vast 360-degree vistas across the 10,000-square-mile intermontane basin toward Thirtynine Mile Mountain and the distant Collegiate Peaks.

name: Ute Trail Pass
park_name: San Isabel National Forest / Royal Gorge BLM
parkName: San Isabel National Forest / Royal Gorge BLM
notes: A rugged 3.0-mile backcountry climb along the historic Ute Trail (Chaffee County Road 175) skirting the southern base of Cameron Mountain near the Whitehorn ghost town. Loose decomposed granite and rocky switchbacks ramp up to 12.3% before topping out at 9,931 feet on the Aspen Ridge divide. The summit unveils a breathtaking panorama of the fourteeners of the Sawatch Range before a thrilling, winding gravel drop plunges 3,000 feet into Salida.

name: Headwaters Hill Approach
notes: Ascends the upper horseshoe curves of the historic Denver & Rio Grande rail bed beneath Headwaters Hill. The thinning subalpine forest reveals sweeping vistas across the Poncha Creek basin as the Continental Divide crest draws within reach.

name: Marshall Pass
landmark: Mount Ouray (13,971 ft) / Continental Divide Crest
notes: Historic 10,842-foot Continental Divide crossing built along Otto Mears' famous 1881 Denver & Rio Grande narrow-gauge railroad grade. The gradual 4% climb winds past the Monarch Crest Trail singletrack junction, rewarding riders with breathtaking panoramic vistas of Mount Ouray before a smooth, roaring descent along Tomichi Creek toward Sargents.

name: Prosser Rock Ridge
park_name: Gunnison National Forest / BLM Gunnison Field Office
parkName: Gunnison National Forest / BLM Gunnison Field Office
notes: A punchy sagebrush gravel rise on County Road 14PP south of Sargents, tracking past the prominent volcanic outcrop of Prosser Rock. The open rangeland offers wide vistas of the Cochetopa Hills and Razor Creek Dome under vast Colorado skies.

name: Old Cochetopa Pass
trail_name: Old Cochetopa Pass Road (USFS 714 / CR NN14)
trailName: Old Cochetopa Pass Road (USFS 714 / CR NN14)
notes: Ascends the historic 10,056-foot saddle of Old Cochetopa Pass along Forest Road 714, a storied mountain thoroughfare surveyed by John C. Frémont in 1853. The firm gravel grade climbs steadily through open ponderosa pine and aspen groves, crossing the Continental Divide between the Gunnison and Rio Grande watersheds.

name: Carnero Creek Ascent
notes: A scenic, sustained 8.1-mile gravel climb tracking the lush riparian corridor of North Carnero Creek into the La Garita Mountains. The gradual 3.8% gradient weaves through beaver dams, expansive cattle ranches, and golden aspen groves before cresting at the shoulder of Storm King Mountain.

name: Climb 115 (Mile 1920.3)
notes: Rolling Cat 4 ascent gaining 30m over 0.6km at an average 5.3% grade (max 11.9%). Traverses unpaved on track.

name: Climb 116 (Mile 1927.3)
notes: Brutal Cat 4 ascent gaining 29m over 0.5km at an average 5.7% grade (max 18.9%). Traverses unpaved on track.

name: Indiana Pass (Course High Point)
park_name: Rio Grande National Forest / San Juan Mountains
landmark: Grayback Mountain (12,605 ft) / Summitville Historic Mining District
parkName: Rio Grande National Forest / San Juan Mountains
notes: At 11,910 ft (3,630 m), Indiana Pass marks the undisputed highest elevation across the entire 2,679-mile Tour Divide. Riders endure a grueling 30-mile net ascent out of Del Norte along Forest Road 380, grinding through the historic, scarred Summitville gold-mining district beneath the towering bulk of Grayback Mountain. Completely exposed above treeline, the summit plateau is notorious for violent afternoon thunderstorms, rapid freeze-ups, and hypothermia hazards for exhausted racers.

name: Stunner Pass
park_name: Rio Grande National Forest / South San Juan Border
parkName: Rio Grande National Forest / South San Juan Border
notes: A rugged 3.4-mile dirt climb scaling the 10,561-foot crest of Stunner Pass along Forest Road 250. Loose rocks and rutted doubletrack test rider handling beneath Klondike Mountain before revealing sweeping views of Platoro Reservoir and the remote historic mining settlement of Platoro below.

name: Valdez Creek Bluff
park_name: Rio Grande National Forest / Conejos Canyon
parkName: Rio Grande National Forest / Conejos Canyon
notes: A gentle gravel roller tracking the cascading waters of the upper Conejos River near the Valdez Trailhead. Towering volcanic cliffs and fragrant pine groves line this peaceful canyon section as the route descends gradually toward Horca.

name: La Manga Pass Ascent
landmark: Pinorealosa Mountain (10,968 ft) / La Manga Pass
notes: A sustained 7.4-mile paved climb winding out of the lower Conejos valley up to the 10,230-foot summit of La Manga Pass. The smooth, sweeping asphalt highway carves through expansive aspen stands and wildflower-carpeted meadows beneath the rugged prominence of Pinorealosa Mountain.

name: Neff Mountain Flank
notes: A short, punchy highway rise hugging the forested eastern shoulder of Neff Mountain between La Manga and Cumbres passes. Riders catch scenic glimpses of the historic narrow-gauge Cumbres & Toltec Scenic Railroad steam line traversing the high subalpine valley.

name: Osier Mesa Rim
park_name: Rio Grande National Forest / Carson National Forest Border
parkName: Rio Grande National Forest / Carson National Forest Border
notes: A rugged 5.1-mile gravel climb on Forest Road 87 scaling the volcanic tablelands of Osier Mesa along the Colorado-New Mexico border. Crossing the state line toward Carson National Forest, the route offers breathtaking overlooks into the deep chasm of Toltec Gorge before approaching the wild Brazos Ridge.

name: Osier Mesa Rim
park_name: Rio Grande National Forest / Carson National Forest Border
parkName: Rio Grande National Forest / Carson National Forest Border
notes: A rugged 5.1-mile gravel climb on Forest Road 87 scaling the volcanic tablelands of Osier Mesa along the Colorado-New Mexico border. Crossing the state line toward Carson National Forest, the route offers breathtaking overlooks into the deep chasm of Toltec Gorge before approaching the wild Brazos Ridge.

name: Brazos Ridge Overlook
notes: Straddles the high subalpine rim of the Tusas Mountains at 10,817 feet, delivering staggering vistas across the sheer 2,000-foot quartzite precipices of the Brazos Cliffs and the pristine Cruces Basin Wilderness. The rocky doubletrack of Forest Road 87 marks a dramatic transition from Colorado soaring peaks to New Mexico ancient volcanic plateaus, challenging riders with lingering snowdrifts in early summer and exposed lightning danger during afternoon monsoons. Rolling along the high alpine mesa, the route treats weary endurance racers to cool mountain breezes before descending into the dry red clay canyons below.

name: Olguin Mesa Summit
notes: Climbs sharply across the northern shoulder of Olguin Mesa along rough, rock-strewn doubletrack sharing the Continental Divide Trail corridor. Punchy pitches exceeding 17% punish fatigued legs amidst dense stands of Engelmann spruce and quaking aspen. The summit crest offers sweeping vistas eastward toward Broke Off Mountain and the Rio San Antonio headwaters before a fast, technical descent on loose volcanic stones.

name: Jawbone Mountain Saddle
notes: Steadily ascends the high volcanic plateau contouring the western flank of Jawbone Mountain on a wide gravel forest road. The 3.6% average gradient allows for a sustained rhythm, though high altitude over 10,000 feet and embedded basalt cobbles require careful line selection. The summit saddle provides panoramic glimpses of the Tusas highlands before diving southward toward Spring Creek.

name: Jawbone Mountain Saddle
notes: Steadily ascends the high volcanic plateau contouring the western flank of Jawbone Mountain on a wide gravel forest road. The 3.6% average gradient allows for a sustained rhythm, though high altitude over 10,000 feet and embedded basalt cobbles require careful line selection. The summit saddle provides panoramic glimpses of the Tusas highlands before diving southward toward Spring Creek.

name: Burned Mountain Pass
notes: Tackles a brisk 6.3% ramp up Spring Creek Road to crest the northern ridge of Burned Mountain just below the 10,000-foot contour. The well-graded unpaved surface winds through mixed pine and aspen groves with views expanding toward Tusas Mountain. Reaching the pass marks the beginning of the long, gradual descent into the historic Vallecitos drainage.

name: Burned Mountain Pass
notes: Tackles a brisk 6.3% ramp up Spring Creek Road to crest the northern ridge of Burned Mountain just below the 10,000-foot contour. The well-graded unpaved surface winds through mixed pine and aspen groves with views expanding toward Tusas Mountain. Reaching the pass marks the beginning of the long, gradual descent into the historic Vallecitos drainage.

name: Kiowa Mountain Pass
notes: Ascends a gentle 5.3% bench along County Road 450 skirting the eastern foothills of Kiowa Mountain. The compacted gravel surface provides fast rolling amidst piñon and ponderosa pines as the route heads toward the upper Vallecitos settlement. Prominent views of Quartzite Peak pale outcrops dominate the northern horizon from the crest.

name: Mesa de la Jarita Ridge
landmark: Mesa de la Jarita / Vallecitos Valley
notes: Climbs steadily out of the Vallecitos River basin on Forest Service Road 44, ascending the pine-studded western flank of Mesa de la Jarita. Gradients hover comfortably around 4% on hardpacked gravel with occasional washboard sections test-riding bike tire pressures. The ridge crest opens up views of the sprawling mesas that separate Vallecitos from the El Rito drainage.

name: El Rito Canyon Divide
landmark: Valle Grande Peak / El Rito Mountains
notes: Follows a sustained 3.4% grade up County Road 247 climbing between Valle Grande Peak and the El Rito Mountains. The wide, dusty gravel road cuts through open ponderosa forest and meadows where free-range cattle frequently graze along the track. Reaching the summit divide at 8,209 feet sets up a sweeping descent toward the red-rock bluffs of El Rito.

name: Cañones Mesa Ascent
notes: A demanding 8.9-mile climb leaving the Rio Chama valley near Abiquiu, ascending through vibrant red-rock canyon country painted by Georgia O Keeffe. The doubletrack surface alternates between deep, tire-sucking red sand and loose volcanic gravel with pitches ramping up to 10.6% under intense desert heat. Topping out on the mesa bench rewards riders with iconic views back over Abiquiu Lake and Sierra Negra.

name: Cerro Pelon Saddle
notes: Steepens noticeably along the southern shoulder of Cerro Pelon, throwing punchy 14% gravel kickers at riders as they transition from scrub juniper into dense montane forest. The rough Forest Road 144 surface demands vigilance over embedded volcanic rocks and rutted wash crossings. Clearings along the upper rim provide striking views of the flat-topped monolith Cerro Pedernal rising majestically to the west.

name: Polvadera Mesa
notes: A legendary, grueling 12-mile epic in the northern Jemez Mountains, ascending over 2,500 vertical feet through the ancient volcanic landscape of the Valles Caldera volcanic field. Forest Road 144 tests endurance with brutal washboard, loose pumice, and rutted red dirt, rising relentlessly from parched piñon canyons into cool subalpine fir and spruce forests beneath 11,217-foot Polvadera Peak. The 10,328-foot summit plateau provides breathtaking 360-degree panoramas extending across the Rio Grande rift to the Sangre de Cristo Range, serving as a defining high-elevation crucible of the New Mexico route.

name: Mesa del Pedregosa Ridge
landmark: La Mesa del Pedregosa / Cerro del Grant
notes: Rolls across the volcanic high plateau of the Jemez Range, kicking up a stiff 6.6% grade across the forested bench of La Mesa del Pedregosa. High altitude above 10,000 feet and chunky dacite rocks keep riders honest despite the short distance. Dense stands of aspen and douglas fir frame glimpses of Cerro del Grant looming directly ahead.

name: Cerro de la Garita Saddle
landmark: Cerro de la Garita / Valles Caldera Border
notes: Traces the undulating rim separating the Jemez volcanic highlands from the Valles Caldera National Preserve near the foot of Cerro de la Garita. The dirt doubletrack rolls at a steady 5% grade through high subalpine meadows dotted with wildflowers in midsummer. At 10,131 feet, the saddle marks one of the highest continuous ridgeline traverses on the New Mexico segment.

name: Cerro del Grant Pass
notes: Ascends the southwestern flank of Cerro del Grant along the remote backcountry thoroughfare known locally as 31 Mile Road. The gravel road winds through thick ponderosa stands and open parklands with ramps up to 8.9% testing loaded touring setups. The 10,210-foot pass provides a commanding view westward across the Rio Puerco headwaters before beginning the descent toward San Pedro Parks.

name: Mining Mountain Pass
park_name: Santa Fe National Forest (San Pedro Parks Flank)
parkName: Santa Fe National Forest (San Pedro Parks Flank)
notes: Grinds up American Creek Road along the northern boundary of the lush San Pedro Parks Wilderness, climbing 774 vertical feet at a consistent 4% grade. The smooth, well-shaded forest road follows rushing mountain streams through verdant aspen glades and pine benches. Cresting the pass beside Mining Mountain and Cerro Jarocito brings crisp alpine air before descending toward the Cuba trailhead corridor.

name: Climb 140 (Mile 2157.7)
notes: Steady Cat 3 ascent gaining 52m over 1.6km at an average 3.3% grade (max 7.0%). Traverses Compacted Hardpack on Unclassified Gravel Road.

name: San Gregorio Ridge
notes: A brisk, rocky pitch on Forest Road 70 passing adjacent to the popular San Gregorio Wilderness trailhead in the Nacimiento Mountains. The doubletrack surface is firm but loose in the corners with grades briefly stiffening to 7.6% amidst towering spruce. Cresting the ridge at 9,245 feet reveals the rugged massifs of Nacimiento Peak and Eureka Mesa.

name: Blue Bird Mesa Pass
notes: A short paved roller on NM Highway 126 negotiating a high gap beneath Blue Bird Mesa just east of Cuba. The 6.3% gradient provides a fast, smooth climb before initiating the dramatic plunge out of the high mountains into the red sandstone badlands of the Rio Puerco valley. Expansive views open up to the arid western horizon and the high-desert plains.

name: Climb 143 (Mile 2245.2)
notes: Rolling Cat 4 ascent gaining 67m over 2.2km at an average 3.1% grade (max 4.9%). Traverses Compacted Hardpack on Unclassified Gravel Road.

name: Mesa Amada Pass
park_name: Cibola National Forest / BLM Rio Puerco District
parkName: Cibola National Forest / BLM Rio Puerco District
notes: Climbs smoothly on paved NM Highway 509 traversing the windswept high-desert gap between Mesa Amada and Mesa de Jaramillo. The steady 5.4% incline cuts across historic uranium mining country north of Ambrosia Lake and Milan. On clear days, the massive, sacred volcanic stratovolcano Mount Taylor dominates the southern skyline above the Grants valley.

name: Mangas Mountain Pass
notes: Ascends through open ponderosa and piñon woodland on Catron County Road A095 south of Pie Town, following the Continental Divide ridge beneath Mangas Mountain. The chunky volcanic gravel surface rolls at an honest 4.2% grade through remote ranching country where water sources are exceptionally sparse. Reaching the 8,278-foot summit provides panoramic vistas across the sprawling Mangas Valley and Luera Range.

name: Bursum Pass
notes: Conquers a sharp 5.9% gravel pitch on Bursum Road winding between Pinon Knob and the Long Canyon Mountains near Beaverhead. The unpaved county road features loose crushed rock and exposed bedrock ribs that demand steady seated power. The saddle overlooks the transition zone where the high Plains of San Agustin collapse into the rugged canyons of the Gila River basin.

name: Kemp Mesa Crest
notes: Punches up a steep 8% grade on the northern approach of North Star Mesa Road, ascending the rugged volcanic caprock of Kemp Mesa. The gravel track is coarse and washboarded, winding past Beaver Points amidst arid piñon-juniper breaks. The crest provides an expansive vantage over the northern threshold of the vast, unforgiving Gila Wilderness.

name: Beaver Creek Divide
notes: Steadily climbs the rolling volcanic tablelands out of the Beaver Creek canyon on Forest Road 150. The road surface consists of compacted clay and embedded river rocks that become notoriously impassable gumbo mud when wet. Reaching the 7,034-foot summit divide offers sweeping views of deep canyon gorges cutting into the heart of the Aldo Leopold Wilderness.

name: Diamond Creek Mesa
landmark: Diamond Creek / East Fork Gila River
notes: A sustained 3-mile grind climbing 666 vertical feet out of the Diamond Creek drainage on the historic North Star Mesa Road. The remote backcountry track features loose gravel, washboard ribs, and unrelenting sun exposure with gradients maxing out at 7.5%. The summit mesa bench rewards riders with cooling breezes and stark vistas of the volcanic plateaus guarding the East Fork of the Gila River.

name: Tom Moore Mesa Saddle
landmark: Tom Moore Mesa / Me Own Hill
notes: A 4.6-mile expedition climb climbing over 900 feet across the remote spine of North Star Mesa between Tom Moore Mesa and Me Own Hill. The doubletrack traverses ancient rhyolite and basalt flows through sparse ponderosa forest where water is virtually nonexistent. Cresting the 7,418-foot saddle provides a breathtaking overlook across the Black Range wilderness to the east.

name: Middle Mesa Crest
notes: Kicks up sharply at a 6.7% grade on Forest Road 150 passing trailheads for Middle Mesa Trail #716 and Tom Moore Canyon. The coarse gravel track requires steady cadence across rocky ledges and loose cobbles. Reaching the summit bench at 7,536 feet reveals dramatic views of the deep cleft of Black Canyon cutting through the volcanic caldera.

name: Rocky Point Pass
notes: A major 5.3-mile ascent gaining over 1,000 feet to crest the southern ramparts of North Star Mesa near the prominent volcanic spire of Rocky Point. Gradients steadily grind between 4% and 7% with steep pitches kicking up to 12.5% through thick ponderosa and gambel oak groves. At 7,956 feet, this summit marks the highest point of the southern Gila traverse, providing immense visual relief and cool mountain air.

name: Rocky Point Pass
notes: A major 5.3-mile ascent gaining over 1,000 feet to crest the southern ramparts of North Star Mesa near the prominent volcanic spire of Rocky Point. Gradients steadily grind between 4% and 7% with steep pitches kicking up to 12.5% through thick ponderosa and gambel oak groves. At 7,956 feet, this summit marks the highest point of the southern Gila traverse, providing immense visual relief and cool mountain air.

name: Loco Mountain Divide
notes: Climbs over rolling volcanic terrain skirting the western foothills of Loco Mountain on Forest Road 150. The gravel surface features sharp 11% switchbacks and loose stony patches that demand careful balance on loaded rigs. The 7,782-foot summit ridge offers panoramic views over the headwaters of the Mimbres River before continuing south.

name: Kelly Mesa Pass
notes: Delivers a punchy 7.4% test on the southern terminus of North Star Mesa Road where it skirts the base of Kelly Mesa. The gravel road surface is rough and rutted from summer thunderstorms with loose rocks scattering across the track. Reaching the pass concludes the grueling North Star Mesa traverse and begins the gradual descent toward Highway 35.

name: Signal Peak Divide
notes: A sprawling 7.5-mile alpine climb ascending 1,365 vertical feet along Forest Road 89, tracing the Continental Divide Trail through the rugged Pinos Altos Range. Rough doubletrack and loose rocky switchbacks with ramps exceeding 12% wind through dense fir, ponderosa, and oak woodland beneath the towering lookout tower on 8,986-foot Signal Peak. The summit crest offers sweeping vistas over the Gila Wilderness before descending toward Meadow Creek.

name: Meadow Creek Saddle
notes: Climbs out of the secluded Meadow Creek drainage along Forest Road 149 beneath the craggy summits of Scott Peak and T X Mountain. The unpaved forest road features smooth gravel through cool, shaded pine groves before breaking out onto an open saddle. The pass marks the final high-mountain divide before dropping toward the historic mining settlement of Pinos Altos.

name: Climb 158 (Mile 2529.3)
notes: Rolling Cat 4 ascent gaining 29m over 0.6km at an average 5.2% grade (max 11.2%). Traverses paved on secondary.

name: Pinos Altos Crest
trail_name: NM Highway 15 (Pinos Altos Road) / Cross Mountain Road
trailName: NM Highway 15 (Pinos Altos Road) / Cross Mountain Road
notes: Ascends through the historic 19th-century gold-mining town of Pinos Altos along NM Highway 15 and Cross Mountain Road. The 5.3% grade winds past rustic log cabins and old adits beneath the distinctive peak of Cross Mountain. The 6,955-foot crest marks the Continental Divide boundary overlooking the expansive Chihuahuan desert plains stretching toward Silver City.

name: Boston Hill Ridge
park_name: Boston Hill Open Space / Silver City Borderlands
parkName: Boston Hill Open Space / Silver City Borderlands
notes: Climbs smoothly on paved and packed-gravel Ridge Road departing the southern outskirts of Silver City. The 5% incline skirts the eastern open space trails of Boston Hill, an ancient mining district noted for silver and iron prospecting. Reaching the ridge summit at 5,853 feet provides a fond final look back at the Pinos Altos mountains as the route enters the arid desert flats.

name: Separ Continental Divide
park_name: Continental Divide Trail Corridor / BLM Las Cruces District
parkName: Continental Divide Trail Corridor / BLM Las Cruces District
notes: Crosses the low Continental Divide crest in the wide desert basin north of Interstate 10 along unpaved Separ Road. The 6% climb rolls across hard-baked caliche gravel flanked by cholla cactus, lechuguilla, and ocotillo with panoramic views of the distant Three Sisters peaks. This subtle desert divide signals the entry into the desolate, heat-scorched expanse of the New Mexico Bootheel.

name: Little Hatchet Mountain Pass
park_name: Little Hatchet Mountains / BLM Las Cruces District
parkName: Little Hatchet Mountains / BLM Las Cruces District
notes: The 177th and final climb of the Tour Divide route, rising 289 vertical feet on rough desert doubletrack skirting the base of 6,614-foot Hachita Peak. Bleaching sun, relentless headwinds, and coarse alluvial wash sand test the final reserves of endurance just 40 miles north of the Mexican border. Cresting this windblown desert pass at 5,049 feet reveals the immense Big Hatchet Mountains standing sentinel over the final descent to Antelope Wells.
